q: A ball is thrown straight up. Air resistance is negligible. What is its acceleration at the highest point?
options: It is reversing direction at that instant
why: Only gravity acts, so the acceleration is $g$ downwards all the time. The velocity is zero at the top, not the acceleration.

q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to $24\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in $8.0\ \text{s}$. How far does it travel in this time?
why: $s = \frac{u+v}{2}t = \frac{0+24}{2}\times 8.0 = 96\ \text{m}$.

q: A runner completes exactly one lap of a $400\ \text{m}$ track in $80\ \text{s}$. What is her average velocity?
why: She ends where she started, so her displacement is zero. $5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is her average speed (distance ÷ time).

q: A stone is dropped from rest. Air resistance is negligible. What is its speed after $2.0\ \text{s}$?
A ball is thrown horizontally at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from a cliff. Air resistance is negligible. What is its horizontal velocity component $1.5\ \text{s}$ later?
why: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal component stays $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. 14.7 is the vertical component and 19.0 the speed.

q: How does significant air resistance change the flight of a projectile, compared with the same launch in a vacuum?
options: The range is unchanged but the maximum height is lower
The path is still symmetrical but the range is shorter
The horizontal velocity stays constant throughout the flight
The range is shorter and the descent is steeper than the ascent
why: Drag keeps reducing the horizontal velocity, so the range is shorter and the path is no longer symmetrical: it falls more steeply than it rose.

q: A book rests on a table. Which force is the Newton’s third law partner of the book’s weight?
options: The normal force of the table on the book
The gravitational force of the book on the Earth
The normal force of the book on the table
The gravitational force of the Earth on the table
why: A third-law pair acts on two different bodies and is the same type of force. The table’s normal force acts on the book too, so it cannot be the partner.

q: A resultant force of $12\ \text{N}$ acts on a $4.0\ \text{kg}$ trolley. What is its acceleration?
A $0.20\ \text{kg}$ ball hits a wall at $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and rebounds at $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse on the ball?
why: The velocity reverses, so $\Delta v = 15 + 10 = 25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $J = m\Delta v = 5.0\ \text{N s}$. $1.0$ forgets the change of direction.

q: A car goes round a circular bend at constant speed. What is the direction of its acceleration?
options: Towards the centre of the bend
None: the speed is constant, so it is not accelerating
why: The direction of the velocity changes, so there is a centripetal acceleration towards the centre. There is no outward force on the car.

q: A $2.0\ \text{kg}$ puck moving east at $3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ collides and sticks to a $2.0\ \text{kg}$ puck moving north at $4.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is their speed afterwards?
why: Momentum components are $6.0$ east and $8.0$ north, so $p = 10\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ and $v = 10/4.0 = 2.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

q: A small sphere falls through oil at terminal speed. Which relation between drag $F_\text{d}$, buoyancy $F_\text{b}$ and weight $mg$ is correct?
why: At terminal speed the resultant force is zero: drag and buoyancy both act upwards and together balance the weight. Forgetting buoyancy gives $F_\text{d} = mg$.

q: A rope at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal pulls a sledge $10\ \text{m}$ along flat ground with a force of $50\ \text{N}$. How much work does the rope do?
why: $W = Fs\cos\theta = 50\times 10\times\cos 60^\circ = 250\ \text{J}$. Only the component along the displacement does work.

q: A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius $r$ at constant speed. The tension is $F$. How much work does the tension do in one revolution?
why: The tension is always perpendicular to the velocity ($\cos 90^\circ = 0$), so it does no work and the kinetic energy stays the same. $2\pi F r$ wrongly multiplies by the distance travelled.

q: A $60\ \text{kg}$ climber rises $5.0\ \text{m}$ up a wall. What is her gain in gravitational potential energy?
why: $\Delta E_\text{p} = mg\Delta h = 60\times 9.8\times 5.0 = 2940\ \text{J}$.

q: A motor takes in $500\ \text{J}$ of electrical energy and wastes $200\ \text{J}$ as thermal energy. What is its efficiency?
why: Useful output is $500 - 200 = 300\ \text{J}$, so $\eta = 300/500 = 0.60$. $0.40$ is the wasted fraction.

q: A car’s speed doubles. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
why: $E_\text{k} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ depends on $v^2$, so doubling $v$ multiplies $E_\text{k}$ by $2^2 = 4$.

q: A car moves at a constant $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ against resistive forces of $600\ \text{N}$. What power does the driving force develop?
why: At constant speed the driving force equals the $600\ \text{N}$ resistance, so $P = Fv = 600\times 20 = 12\ \text{kW}$. The resultant force is zero, but the driving force is not.

q: A force of $40\ \text{N}$ is applied perpendicular to a spanner, $0.25\ \text{m}$ from the bolt. What is the torque about the bolt?
why: $\tau = Fr\sin\theta = 40\times 0.25\times\sin 90^\circ = 10.0\ \text{N m}$.

q: A spinning skater pulls her arms in. Friction is negligible. What happens?
options: Angular momentum increases and angular velocity increases
Angular momentum is constant and angular velocity decreases
Rotational kinetic energy is constant and angular velocity increases
Angular momentum is constant and angular velocity increases
why: No external torque, so $L = I\omega$ is constant; $I$ falls, so $\omega$ rises. $E_\text{k} = L^2/2I$ increases: she does work pulling her arms in.

q: Two $2.0\ \text{kg}$ point masses are each $0.50\ \text{m}$ from an axis. What is the moment of inertia of the pair about that axis?
why: $I = \Sigma mr^2 = 2\times 2.0\times 0.50^2 = 1.0\ \text{kg m}^2$.

q: A wheel starts from rest with a uniform angular acceleration of $4.0\ \text{rad s}^{-2}$. What is its angular velocity after $3.0\ \text{s}$?
why: $\omega_\text{f} = \omega_\text{i} + \alpha t = 0 + 4.0\times 3.0 = 12\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. $18$ is the angular displacement in radians.

q: A solid disc and a ring have the same mass and radius. Equal torques act on each from rest. Which has the larger angular acceleration?
options: The disc, because more of its mass is close to the axis
The ring, because its mass is far from the axis
why: The disc’s mass is closer to the axis, so its moment of inertia is smaller and $\alpha = \tau/I$ is larger. Same mass does not mean same $I$.

q: A flywheel with moment of inertia $2.0\ \text{kg m}^2$ spins at $10\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. What is its rotational kinetic energy?
why: $E_\text{k} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times 2.0\times 10^2 = 100\ \text{J}$. $200$ forgets the $\frac{1}{2}$; $20$ is $I\omega$, the angular momentum.

q: A train moves at $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. A passenger walks towards the front at $2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ relative to the train. Using Galilean relativity, what is her speed relative to the ground?
why: In Galilean relativity velocities in the same direction simply add: $30 + 2.0 = 32\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. $28$ would be for walking towards the back.

q: What is the Lorentz factor $\gamma$ for a speed of $0.60c$?
Which observer measures the proper time interval between two events?
options: The observer for whom both events happen at the same place
The observer who is at rest relative to the Earth
The observer who measures the longest time interval
Any observer moving much slower than light
why: Proper time is measured in the frame where the two events occur at the same position. It is the shortest interval any observer measures, not the longest.

q: A tunnel has a proper length of $600\ \text{m}$. What length does an observer in a rocket moving through it at $0.80c$ measure?
why: $\gamma = 1/0.60$, so $L = L_0/\gamma = 600\times 0.60 = 360\ \text{m}$. Moving lengths are contracted.

q: On a space–time diagram, a particle’s world line makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the $ct$ axis. What is its speed?
why: $\tan\theta = v/c$, so $v = c\tan 30^\circ = 0.58c$. $0.50c$ uses $\sin$; $1.73c$ measures the angle from the $x$ axis.

q: Lightning strikes the front and back of a moving train at the same time in the ground frame. In the train’s frame, which strike happens first?
options: It depends on where the observer sits on the train
why: Simultaneity is relative: from $t' = \gamma(t - vx/c^2)$ the event further forward (larger $x$) has the earlier $t'$. Where an observer sits changes when light arrives, not when the strikes happen in that frame.
